author: Jack Gurley
title: Remembering Hurricane Rita 20 years later - NewsBreak
text:
By Jack Gurley ,
35 minutes ago
TYLER, Texas ( KETK )- Today marks 20 years since Hurricane Rita tore through the Texas-Louisiana border, bringing devastating winds and extreme rainfall
“Rita actually was then and even to this day the strongest hurricane ever recorded in the Gulf,” East Texas Storm Team Meteorologist Brayden Siau said.
Hurricane Rita hit just 26 days after Hurricane Katrina left Louisiana in shambles. Mass panic led to mass evacuations, time ticking away as it barreled toward land.
“2 and a half to 3 million people evacuating, and that just caused chaos,” Siau said. ” More people died in the evacuation from Rita than in the storm itself.”
East Texas judge retires after 47 years of service Twenty years later, Katherine Doyle reflects on the days leading up to the moment when she was a freshman in high school, leaving everything behind to find safety with her family.
“I can remember very vividly the whole thing,” Hurricane Rita storm survivor Kathryn Doyle said. “It was my mom and I in the car with our two dogs, and then I had two older brothers who were in their vehicles, and we were all just stuck in traffic.”
Waiting 17 long hours stuck in bumper-to-bumper traffic, remembering the exact route they took to get out eventually.
“They do something called contraflow, so they turn the interstate into one way,” Doyle said. “So you can only go one direction, both ways of the interstate out of town.”
Not everyone could evacuate, though some stayed behind waiting out the long, stormy night.
“That’s really what made Rita a lot scarier, because it hit in the middle of the night,” Siau said. “I do remember just hearing the sound of the wind outside and the pitch black.”
At just three years old, meteorologist Bryden Siau recalls the long night vividly, with wind blowing and trees crashing to the ground.
“You can just hear it, the wind would blow and then you would hear this noise and like a boom when it hit the ground,” Siau said. “You couldn’t see anything until the storm finally passed, and we went outside, and I mean, it just looked like a bomb had gone off. That’s the best way to describe it.”
East Texas WWII veteran, community leader celebrates 99th birthday When people returned to their hometowns, they looked completely different homes gone, trees uprooted, and debris left scattered across the area.
“The leaves literally had been ripped off the trees,” Siau said. “A lot of trees, especially the pine trees, had been snapped in half and were kind of just split in two.”
A day residents who survived it won’t ever forget, creating a stronger respect for the power it brought and a more profound empathy for those who will inevitably face it again.
“It stuck with me, I also wanted to use it differently,” Siau said. “While it interested me, I also wanted to one day be able to be the person who was helping these people, forecasting for them, telling them that these storms are coming.”
